rows.identity: an independent-minded advocate for fair access who helps shape organisational information ethics and campaigns for laws protecting users

rows.knowledge: the distinct information needs of disciplines from STEM to law, debates on decolonising information practice and the research methods that produce evidence for the profession
rows.identity: a strategic leader of library and archive services who advocates for ethical practice and judges each initiative by its effect on communities and users

digest.definition: A family of related disciplines concerned with representing, organising and communicating knowledge so that anyone can find, use, judge and share the information they need
distinctiveFeatures: A family of related disciplines concerned with representing, organising and communicating knowledge so that anyone can find, use, judge and share the information they need
Practice-based and vocational as well as academic, with many entering through postgraduate study; the field is mostly studied at postgraduate level
Information itself is the object of study, so students turn a critical eye on their own use of it and on how sources change
Rests on distinctive ethical foundations set out by the professional bodies and on long-standing law, such as copyright, equalities, data protection and freedom of information
Social justice runs through it: tackling bias in collections and systems, decolonising practice and working for fair access for groups once marginalised
Combines theory with practice through case studies, problem-based learning, placements and partnerships with the profession
Technologically fluent: metadata, repositories, user experience, data and, increasingly, AI tools, always with ethical oversight
Careers span libraries in many sectors, archives and records work, curation, information governance and knowledge management

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: Fair, unbiased access is the ethical core of the field: graduates work against bias in collections and knowledge systems, decolonise practice and serve marginalised groups (D1, 1.7 to 1.10)
Accessibility is both how courses are run (varied, flexible, inclusive methods) and what graduates build (accessible systems, spaces and interfaces) (D1, 1.11; 2.9; 3.9)
Preserving and giving access to recorded knowledge and heritage is itself a contribution to sustainability, with the UN goals and sector initiatives named (D1, 1.12 to 1.14)
Enterprise is treated as core: service design, innovation and practical action, with authentic assessment and the professional skills base behind it (D1, 1.15 to 1.19)
AI is both a subject of critical, ethical study and a set of tools for metadata, discovery and services; students learn to use it and to teach others about it (D1, 1.20; 1.21)

headingPath: Distinctive features of Librarianship, Information, Knowledge, Records and Archive Management

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject at any award
statements.about: reflecting on their own information use and ethics
statements.paraphrase: Since information is the very thing the subject studies, students must look back on their own experience and ethical priorities as people who use information.

forPractitioner.text: Give students structured occasions to examine their own habits and ethical priorities as information users: the subject requires it, because information is what they study.

forBeneficiary.text: You must reflect on how you yourself use information and on the ethical priorities you bring to it, because information is the thing you are studying.

headingPath: Distinctive features of Librarianship, Information, Knowledge, Records and Archive Management

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject at any award
statements.about: how information shifts and why it needs appraising
statements.paraphrase: Students should be able to build, and show, an understanding that information keeps changing, that how it is used has effects, and that it has to be judged afresh as society and technology move on.

forPractitioner.text: Students should come to understand, and be able to show, that information is fluid, that its use has consequences and that appraisal must keep pace with social and technical change.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to show that you understand how information changes over time, how its use affects people, and why it needs judging again as society and technology change.

headingPath: Distinctive features of Librarianship, Information, Knowledge, Records and Archive Management

statements.about: core skills for joint and combined honours students
statements.paraphrase: Undergraduates taking the subject within a joint or combined degree, including major and minor routes, will attain the central subject-specific and generic skills set out here and gain others from their second subject.

forPractitioner.text: In a joint or combined honours course, students will reach the core of the subject-specific and generic skills set out here; the other subject adds further skills, so map which core items each route covers.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study this field as part of a joint or combined degree, you will gain its core subject and general skills, plus further skills from the other subject you take.

statements.about: a system for student input to course monitoring
statements.paraphrase: Students' views come first in monitoring and review, and the awarding body will run a system through which students feed into monitoring and evaluation.

forPractitioner.text: The awarding body will have a working route, such as a staff and student liaison forum, for students to contribute to course monitoring and evaluation.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider and the people who run the course, not a standard the student reaches

headingPath: Distinctive features of Librarianship, Information, Knowledge, Records and Archive Management

statements.paraphrase: In periodic review the institution will bring in external reviewers, for an outside view of planned changes and to confirm that threshold standards are met and content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Plan periodic review with external reviewers who will give an independent view of proposed changes and confirm that threshold standards are met and the content fits the subject.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider and the people who run the course, not a standard the student reaches

statements.appliesTo: assessment in courses of the subject
statements.paraphrase: Assessment will include tasks, such as portfolios, synoptic work and self-reflection, through which students build and show professional competence.

forPractitioner.text: Include assessment, for instance a portfolio, a synoptic task or a self-reflective piece, in which students grow and evidence professional competencies.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be assessed through tasks such as portfolios, synoptic work and self-reflection, which let you build and show your professional skills.

statements.appliesTo: assessment in courses of the subject
statements.paraphrase: Assessment will include chances to evaluate, reflexively and critically, professional and sector identity, professional growth and the student's own learning, through reflections, presentations or case studies.

forPractitioner.text: Include assessment, such as critical reflections, presentations or case studies, where students evaluate their professional and sector identity, their development and their learning journey.

forBeneficiary.text: You will have assessments, such as reflective writing, presentations or case studies, where you look critically at your professional identity, your development and how your learning has gone.

statements.appliesTo: assessment in courses of the subject
statements.paraphrase: Assessment will include authentic tasks in which students apply their learning to make a real contribution in a workplace, sector or community setting, through projects, placements or project documents.

forPractitioner.text: Include authentic assessment, such as practical projects, placements or project documentation, where students apply learning and make a genuine contribution in a sector, workplace or community setting.

forBeneficiary.text: You will have assessments set in real workplaces, the sector or the community, such as projects or placements, where what you do makes a genuine contribution.

statements.appliesTo: assessment in courses of the subject
statements.paraphrase: Assessment will include tasks, such as group projects, presentations or portfolios, that show students can work well with others in a team.

forPractitioner.text: Include assessed group work, such as joint projects, presentations or portfolios, through which students show they can collaborate effectively.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be assessed on how well you work in a group, for example through team projects, joint presentations or shared portfolios.

statements.appliesTo: assessment in courses of the subject
statements.paraphrase: Assessment will include tasks showing that students can use digital technologies, generative AI among them, to make websites, databases, catalogues, presentations, posters, social media outputs or other digital content.

forPractitioner.text: Include assessment in which students produce digital content (websites, databases, online catalogues, posters, social media outputs and the like) and may use generative AI in doing so.

forBeneficiary.text: You will have assessments where you make digital content, such as a website, a database, an online catalogue or social media posts, and you may use generative AI tools to help.

statements.appliesTo: assessment in courses of the subject
statements.paraphrase: Assessment will include research tasks, gathering primary data or interrogating and synthesising secondary data at length, analysing it and presenting the findings.

forPractitioner.text: Include an assessed research task in which students collect primary data or work extensively with secondary data, analyse it and present what they find.

forBeneficiary.text: You will carry out assessed research, collecting your own data or working closely with existing data, analysing it and presenting what you found.

statements.about: using Annex D to judge achievement above threshold
statements.paraphrase: Each institution sets its own way of deciding what evidence shows achievement beyond the threshold, and should consult Annex D of the UK qualifications frameworks (the classification descriptions) in doing so.

forPractitioner.text: When deciding what evidence marks achievement above the threshold, use your own method but consult Annex D of the Frameworks (the classification descriptions for honours degrees).

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider and the people who run the course, not a standard the student reaches

statements.paraphrase: Where an institution writes competence standards under the Equality Act 2010 into a programme specification, it should follow the latest guidance of the Equality and Human Rights Commission.

forPractitioner.text: If you set competence standards (in the Equality Act 2010 sense) for a programme, follow the current Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance; the threshold standards here are not competence standards.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider and the people who run the course, not a standard the student reaches

statements.about: applying knowledge in structured, guided settings
statements.paraphrase: Part of those concepts and practices: honours students should be able to use their knowledge where the setting is structured and guidance is given.

forPractitioner.text: Honours students should be able to put knowledge to work in structured contexts with guidance; at this level the setting is framed for them.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to use what you know in tasks that are clearly structured and where you have guidance.

statements.about: systematic grasp of the course's core knowledge
statements.paraphrase: At the honours threshold, students should be able to show a systematic grasp of the central knowledge their course covers.

forPractitioner.text: By the end of an honours course, students should be able to show ordered, systematic understanding of the course's core knowledge; teach and assess the whole of it, not isolated topics.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, you should be able to show a well-organised understanding of the main knowledge your course covers.

statements.paraphrase: Honours students should be able to analyse and judge information inside frameworks already set for the task.

forPractitioner.text: Honours students should analyse and evaluate information within established frameworks, rather than devising their own.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to analyse and judge information using frameworks that are already set out for you.

statements.about: using core concepts in clearly bounded cases
statements.paraphrase: They should be able to grasp and use the subject's key concepts, principles and practices in clearly bounded situations, choosing processes, materials and techniques with judgement.

forPractitioner.text: Honours students should apply the subject's key concepts, principles and practices to clearly framed cases, exercising judgement over which processes, materials and techniques to use.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to understand and use the main ideas, principles and practices of your subject in clearly set-out situations, choosing sensibly which methods and materials to use.

statements.about: using tools and methods in practice
statements.paraphrase: Honours students should be able to use the subject's tools, technologies and methods in practical settings.

forPractitioner.text: Honours students should use tools, technologies and methodologies of the field in practical settings, such as labs, projects or placements.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to use the tools, technologies and methods of your field in practical work.

statements.paraphrase: Honours graduates at the threshold, the third class, will have shown some proficiency in most, not all, of the attributes the statement lists.

forPractitioner.text: Read the honours lists as a profile: a third-class graduate will have shown some proficiency in most of the listed attributes, not every one of them.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum level for an honours degree (a third), you will have shown some skill in most, though not all, of the abilities set out for your subject.

statements.about: tackling bias in collections, systems and services
statements.paraphrase: At the honours threshold, graduates should be able to plan and carry out approaches that expose and reduce bias in collections, systems and services, so that people are fairly represented and obstacles to access come down.

forPractitioner.text: By the end of an honours course, students should be able to plan and carry out approaches that expose and reduce bias in collections, systems and services, so that people are fairly represented and obstacles to access come down; give them a task that lets them show it.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, you should be able to plan and carry out ways of spotting and correcting bias in collections, catalogues and services, so that everyone is fairly represented and can reach what they need.

statements.about: a working commitment to access and equity
statements.paraphrase: At the honours threshold, graduates should be able to show, across research, communication and teamwork, that they hold accessibility and fairness as commitments, and act to clear away what blocks access and participation.

forPractitioner.text: By the end of an honours course, students should be able to show, across research, communication and teamwork, that they hold accessibility and fairness as commitments, and act to clear away what blocks access and participation; give them a task that lets them show it.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, you should be able to show in all your work, research and teamwork included, that you care about access and fairness, and take steps to remove what stops people finding information or joining in.

statements.about: inclusive physical and online spaces and collections
statements.paraphrase: At the honours threshold, graduates should be able to shape library spaces and collections, in person and online, so that they serve people with a wide spread of abilities and needs.

forPractitioner.text: By the end of an honours course, students should be able to shape library spaces and collections, in person and online, so that they serve people with a wide spread of abilities and needs; give them a task that lets them show it.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, you should be able to design library spaces and collections, physical and online, that work well for people with different abilities and needs.

statements.paraphrase: At the honours threshold, graduates should be able to work with community groups and teachers to advance academic, data, digital, media and information literacies that serve scholarship and learning through life.

forPractitioner.text: By the end of an honours course, students should be able to work with community groups and teachers to advance academic, data, digital, media and information literacies that serve scholarship and learning through life; give them a task that lets them show it.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, you should be able to team up with community groups and teachers to help people build their academic, data, digital, media and information skills, for study and for learning through life.

statements.about: human rights, equality and fair access to information
statements.paraphrase: At the honours threshold, graduates should be able to debate critically how information provision bears on human rights and equality, question structural inequality and bias (by race, gender or disability) in knowledge systems, and argue for fair access for groups once pushed aside.

forPractitioner.text: By the end of an honours course, students should be able to debate critically how information provision bears on human rights and equality, question structural inequality and bias (by race, gender or disability) in knowledge systems, and argue for fair access for groups once pushed aside; give them a task that lets them show it.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, you should be able to discuss critically how information services affect human rights and equality, challenge bias built into knowledge systems, such as bias by race, gender or disability, and speak up for fair access for groups who have been left out.

statements.about: freedom of access and open access
statements.paraphrase: At the honours threshold, graduates should be able to argue that free access to information is a basic human right, and make the case for open access to knowledge and for the skills and systems that make access possible.

forPractitioner.text: By the end of an honours course, students should be able to argue that free access to information is a basic human right, and make the case for open access to knowledge and for the skills and systems that make access possible; give them a task that lets them show it.

statements.about: teaching and outreach for critical thinking

forPractitioner.text: In postgraduate certificate, diploma and master's courses, give students room to show they can plan teaching and outreach that build critical thinking, media literacy and safe, responsible participation online; at threshold they will have shown most such attributes to some degree.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your postgraduate course, you will have shown that you can plan teaching and outreach sessions that help people think critically, read the media well and take part safely and responsibly online.

statements.about: user data and metrics for evidence-based improvement
statements.paraphrase: At the master's threshold, graduates will have shown the ability to gather and analyse data on users, service performance and sector trends, and use it to ground decisions in evidence and keep improving.

forPractitioner.text: In postgraduate certificate, diploma and master's courses, give students room to show they can gather and analyse data on users, service performance and sector trends, and use it to ground decisions in evidence and keep improving; at threshold they will have shown most such attributes to some degree.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your postgraduate course, you will have shown that you can gather and analyse data about users, how services perform and trends in the sector, and use it to make decisions and keep improving.

statements.about: a culture of experiment in services
statements.paraphrase: At the master's threshold, graduates will have shown the ability to build a habit of experiment, testing how new technologies and approaches could improve information services.

forPractitioner.text: In postgraduate certificate, diploma and master's courses, give students room to show they can build a habit of experiment, testing how new technologies and approaches could improve information services; at threshold they will have shown most such attributes to some degree.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your postgraduate course, you will have shown that you can encourage a habit of trying things out, testing how new technologies and ideas could improve information services.

statements.paraphrase: At the master's threshold, graduates will have shown the ability to look actively for chances to be entrepreneurial, creating new information products, services or ventures.

forPractitioner.text: In postgraduate certificate, diploma and master's courses, give students room to show they can look actively for chances to be entrepreneurial, creating new information products, services or ventures; at threshold they will have shown most such attributes to some degree.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your postgraduate course, you will have shown that you can look out for chances to be enterprising and create new information products, services or businesses.

statements.about: AI tools for automated tasks, with ethical oversight
statements.paraphrase: At the master's threshold, graduates will have shown the ability to try out AI tools for automated work such as metadata generation and recommender systems, keeping ethical oversight in place.

forPractitioner.text: In postgraduate certificate, diploma and master's courses, give students room to show they can try out AI tools for automated work such as metadata generation and recommender systems, keeping ethical oversight in place; at threshold they will have shown most such attributes to some degree.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your postgraduate course, you will have shown that you can try out AI tools for automatic tasks, such as creating metadata or recommending resources, while keeping an ethical check on how they are used.

statements.paraphrase: At the master's threshold, graduates will have shown the ability to stand up for freedom of thought and expression, for the privacy of personal data, and for open access to information and data.

forPractitioner.text: In postgraduate certificate, diploma and master's courses, give students room to show they can stand up for freedom of thought and expression, for the privacy of personal data, and for open access to information and data; at threshold they will have shown most such attributes to some degree.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your postgraduate course, you will have shown that you can stand up for people's freedom of thought and expression, for the privacy of their data, and for open access to information and data.

statements.paraphrase: At the master's threshold, graduates will have shown the ability to help shape organisational policy on ethical information practice, responsible data governance and the rights of users.

forPractitioner.text: In postgraduate certificate, diploma and master's courses, give students room to show they can help shape organisational policy on ethical information practice, responsible data governance and the rights of users; at threshold they will have shown most such attributes to some degree.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your postgraduate course, you will have shown that you can help write your organisation's policies on the ethical use of information, careful handling of data and the rights of its users.

statements.about: advocacy for fair access and privacy law
statements.paraphrase: At the master's threshold, graduates will have shown the ability to take part in local and national campaigning for laws that widen fair access to information and protect users' privacy.

forPractitioner.text: In postgraduate certificate, diploma and master's courses, give students room to show they can take part in local and national campaigning for laws that widen fair access to information and protect users' privacy; at threshold they will have shown most such attributes to some degree.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your postgraduate course, you will have shown that you can take part in local and national campaigns for laws that give people fair access to information and protect their privacy.

statements.paraphrase: At the master's threshold, graduates will have shown the ability to use strategic analysis and leadership to deliver, track and judge initiatives and grasp their effect on the communities or users concerned.

forPractitioner.text: In postgraduate certificate, diploma and master's courses, give students room to show they can use strategic analysis and leadership to deliver, track and judge initiatives and grasp their effect on the communities or users concerned; at threshold they will have shown most such attributes to some degree.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your postgraduate course, you will have shown that you can use strategic thinking and leadership to run, track and judge projects, and understand what they mean for the people they serve.

statements.about: using results to plan future services
statements.paraphrase: At the master's threshold, graduates will have shown the ability to draw on results to shape future services and outreach.

forPractitioner.text: In postgraduate certificate, diploma and master's courses, give students room to show they can draw on results to shape future services and outreach; at threshold they will have shown most such attributes to some degree.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your postgraduate course, you will have shown that you can use what your projects achieved to shape future services and outreach.

statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show a full grasp of the research techniques their own research or advanced study needs, and a sound use of fitting research philosophies and methods.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show a full grasp of the research techniques their own research or advanced study needs, and a sound use of fitting research philosophies and methods; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show a full understanding of the research techniques your own research needs, and that you can use suitable research philosophies and methods.

statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show originality in the way they put knowledge to use.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show originality in the way they put knowledge to use; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show originality in how you put your knowledge to use.

statements.about: research as evidence for professional practice
statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show a working grasp of how established research and enquiry produce and test evidence that improves professional practice.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show a working grasp of how established research and enquiry produce and test evidence that improves professional practice; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show that you understand in practice how research methods produce and test evidence that improves professional work.

statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show that they can carry through, by independent study, a substantial critical piece of empirical research, a work-based project, a major review or a case study, which may add to research or solve a workplace problem.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show that they can carry through, by independent study, a substantial critical piece of empirical research, a work-based project, a major review or a case study, which may add to research or solve a workplace problem; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show that you can complete on your own a substantial piece of critical research, a work-based project, a major review or a case study, which might add to research or solve a problem at work.

statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show a conceptual grasp that lets them judge current research and advanced scholarship in the field critically.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show a conceptual grasp that lets them judge current research and advanced scholarship in the field critically; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show an understanding of ideas deep enough to judge current research and advanced study in your field critically.

statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show a conceptual grasp that lets them assess and critique research methods and, where fitting, put forward new hypotheses, which may mean knowing methods from neighbouring fields.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show a conceptual grasp that lets them assess and critique research methods and, where fitting, put forward new hypotheses, which may mean knowing methods from neighbouring fields; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show an understanding of ideas deep enough to assess and critique research methods and, where it fits, suggest new hypotheses, perhaps drawing on methods from related subjects.

statements.about: complex issues, judgement and clear communication
statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show that they can handle complex issues both methodically and inventively, judge soundly when data are incomplete, and explain their conclusions plainly to expert and general audiences.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show that they can handle complex issues both methodically and inventively, judge soundly when data are incomplete, and explain their conclusions plainly to expert and general audiences; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show that you can handle complex issues methodically and creatively, judge well when you lack some of the data, and explain your conclusions clearly to experts and non-experts.

statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show that they direct themselves and work with creativity and originality.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show that they direct themselves and work with creativity and originality; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show that you direct your own work and bring creativity and originality to it.

statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show skill in leading and advocating, aware of the shifting internal and external factors that bear on both.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show skill in leading and advocating, aware of the shifting internal and external factors that bear on both; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show that you can lead and speak up for a cause, aware of the changing pressures inside and outside an organisation that affect both.

statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show that they can use tools and processes to network effectively across the world.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show that they can use tools and processes to network effectively across the world; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show that you can use tools and processes to build useful professional networks worldwide.

statements.paraphrase: Master's graduates should be able to show that they can question current practice and make the case for the changes they propose.

forPractitioner.text: Postgraduate students should be able to show that they can question current practice and make the case for the changes they propose; build it into the research and project work of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's course, you should be able to show that you can question how things are done now and make the case for the changes you propose.
